newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans oppose coalition tax plan-SPD's Lafontaine.
newsitem.headline: Germans oppose coalition tax plan-SPD's Lafontaine.

text.p: A majority of Germans opposes plans by the coalition government to slash taxes for top earners as part of a tax reform plan, Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Friday.

"A large majority simply does not understand why Chancellor Helmut Kohl calls for wage restraint and the coalition at the same time demands a reform which would bring tax cuts of 20,000 to 30,000 marks a year for the rich," Lafontaine said.
"That is more than these poor people who are fighting for their jobs earn in a whole year," he told parliament in a debate on how to tackle Germany's record post-war unemployment.

The debate was the first opportunity for government and opposition leaders to face up to each other after the resolution on Thursday of a dispute over coal subsidies which had led the SPD to break off cross-party talks on tax reforms.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday was presenting a legislative draft of a 30 billion mark package of tax cuts which would slash income and corporate taxes in a drive to put Germany's 4.7 million unemployed back to work.

Lafontaine has already made rejoining the tax talks conditional on new government proposals to cut social security charges and to lighten the tax load on ordinary workers and their families next year.

He also called on the coalition parties to explain how they planned to plug a 50 billion mark financing gap left by Waigel's tax draft. "If the SPD and coalition are to talk again, this question must be answered," Lafontaine said.
The SPD chief also warned the government against attempting to impose any further cuts in welfare benefits.
"If you really plan further cuts in social security, then at least say so openly," Lafontaine said.
